title: Op-Amp Lab
description: Ideal op-amp circuits with random resistors and inputs: inverting, non-inverting, summing, difference and cascades.

study.title: Ideal op-amp rules
study.body: With negative feedback, an ideal op amp drives its output so that the two inputs are at the same voltage (**virtual short**), and no current flows into either input. Write KCL at the inverting input using these two rules and solve for $v_o$.

study.title: Inverting and non-inverting
study.body: Inverting: the input current $v_{in}/R_1$ must all flow through $R_f$, so $v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_{in}$ and the source sees $R_1$. Non-inverting: $R_1$ and $R_f$ divide $v_o$ back to $v_{in}$, so the gain is $1 + R_f/R_1$ and the input draws no current.

study.title: Summing and difference
study.body: Summing: each input sends $v_k/R_k$ into the virtual-ground node; the sum flows through $R_f$. Difference: the + input sits at the divider voltage $v_2\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$; with $R_4/R_3 = R_f/R_1$ only the difference $v_2 - v_1$ is amplified.

study.title: Common mistakes
study.body:
- Dropping the minus sign of the inverting gain, or writing $R_f/R_1$ instead of $1 + R_f/R_1$ for the non-inverting gain.
- Assuming the output current equals the feedback current: with a load the output also supplies $v_o/R_L$.
- Forgetting saturation: a real op amp cannot exceed its supplies (here ±12 V); an ideal-model answer beyond that means the circuit clips.

steps.prompt: Inverting amplifier with an ideal op amp.

ask.explanation: Virtual ground at the − input, so $i = v_{in}/R_1$ flows on through $R_f$: $v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_{in}$ = −{{Rf/R1||3}} · ({{Vin|V}}) = **{{V_U1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current through $R_f$.
ask.explanation: No current enters the op amp, so $R_f$ carries the input current: $|i| = |v_{in}|/R_1$ = {{abs(Vin)|V}} / {{R1|Ω}} = **{{abs(I_Rf)|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the input resistance $v_{in}/i_{in}$ seen by the source.
ask.explanation: The − input is a virtual ground, so the source sees just $R_1$: $R_{in}$ = **{{Vin/I_Vin|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: Because of the virtual short, current flows directly from the + input to the − input of an ideal op amp.
steps.explanation: The virtual short means $v_+ = v_-$, **not** a real connection: an ideal op amp draws zero current at both inputs. The equal voltages are maintained by the output through the feedback network.

steps.prompt: Non-inverting amplifier with an ideal op amp.

ask.explanation: Virtual short: $v_- = v_{in}$. $R_1$ and $R_f$ form a divider from $v_o$: $v_{in} = v_o\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_f}$, so $v_o = \left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_1}\right)v_{in}$ = {{1+Rf/R1||3}} · ({{Vin|V}}) = **{{V_U1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current through $R_f$.
ask.explanation: $v_- = v_{in}$, so $R_1$ carries $|v_{in}|/R_1$ = {{abs(Vin)/R1|A}}. No current enters the − input, so the same current flows in $R_f$: **{{abs(I_Rf)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has $R_1$ = 2 kΩ (to ground) and $R_f$ = 10 kΩ. What is its gain?
steps.explanation: $1 + R_f/R_1$ = 1 + 10/2 = 6. Gain 5 forgets the 1 (that is the inverting magnitude); −5 is the inverting gain.

steps.prompt: Ideal op amp. Tap every resistor that has **no effect** on $v_o$.
steps.explanation:
- No current flows into the + input of an ideal op amp, so $R_s$ has no voltage drop: $v_+ = v_{in}$.
- An ideal op amp sets $v_o$ whatever load it drives, so $R_L$ only changes the output current.
The gain is set by $R_1$ and $R_f$: $v_o = \left(1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}\right) v_{in}$.

steps.prompt: Summing amplifier with an ideal op amp.

ask.explanation: Virtual ground at the − input: $i_1 = V_1/R_1$ = {{V1/R1|A}}, $i_2 = V_2/R_2$ = {{V2/R2|A}}. Their sum flows through $R_f$: $v_o = -R_f(i_1+i_2)$ = **{{V_U1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current through $R_f$.
ask.explanation: KCL at the virtual ground: $i_f = V_1/R_1 + V_2/R_2$ = {{V1/R1|A}} + ({{V2/R2|A}}), so $|i_f|$ = **{{abs(I_Rf)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: What input resistance does the source see in an ideal non-inverting amplifier?
steps.explanation: The source connects only to the + input, which draws no current, so $R_{in} \to \infty$. That is the main advantage over the inverting amplifier, whose input resistance is $R_1$.

ask.explanation: The + input is a divider: $v_+ = V_2\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$ = {{V_R4|V}}. Virtual short: $v_- = v_+$. KCL at $v_-$: $v_o = v_+\left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_1}\right) - \frac{R_f}{R_1}V_1$ = **{{V_U1|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the voltage at the inverting input.
ask.explanation: Virtual short: $v_- = v_+ = V_2\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$ = **{{V_R4|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current through $R_f$.
ask.explanation: $v_- = V_2\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}$ = {{V_R4|V}}. $R_1$ carries $(V_1 - v_-)/R_1$ and all of it continues through $R_f$: $|i|$ = **{{abs(I_Rf)|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the output of the first stage.
ask.explanation: Stage 1 is inverting: $v_{o1} = -\frac{R_{f1}}{R_1}v_{in}$ = −{{Rf1/R1||3}} · ({{Vin|V}}) = **{{V_U1|V}}**.
$v_{o1} = -\frac{R_{f1}}{R_1}v_{in}$ = {{V_U1|V}}. An ideal op-amp output is a perfect source, so stage 2 is not loaded: $v_o = -\frac{R_{f2}}{R_2}v_{o1}$ = **{{V_U2|V}}**.
The gains multiply: $\left(-\frac{R_{f1}}{R_1}\right)\left(-\frac{R_{f2}}{R_2}\right)$ = {{Rf1/R1||3}} · {{Rf2/R2||3}} = **{{V_U2/Vin||3}}** (two inversions cancel).

steps.prompt: In an ideal inverting amplifier, the current in $R_f$ equals the current in $R_1$.
steps.explanation: KCL at the − input: the op amp input draws nothing, so whatever flows through $R_1$ must continue through $R_f$.

steps.prompt: An inverting amplifier drives a load $R_L$.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current the op-amp output must supply.
ask.explanation: $v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_{in}$ = {{V_U1|V}}. The output feeds the load ($v_o/R_L$ = {{V_U1/RL|A}}) and also sinks the feedback current: $i_o = \frac{v_o}{R_L} + \frac{v_o}{R_f}$ (the − input is at 0 V), so $|i_o|$ = **{{abs(I_RL-I_Rf)|A}}**.
$v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_{in}$ = {{V_U1|V}} (the load does not change $v_o$ for an ideal op amp). $P = v_o^2/R_L$ = **{{P_RL|W}}**.
$v_o = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}v_{in}$ = **{{V_U1|V}}**, independent of $R_L$ because the ideal output is a perfect voltage source.

steps.prompt: A difference amplifier (inverting input via $R_1$, feedback $R_f$, non-inverting input via $R_3$ with $R_4$ to ground) amplifies only $v_2 - v_1$ when…
steps.explanation: $v_o = v_2\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4}\left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_1}\right) - v_1\frac{R_f}{R_1}$. With $R_4/R_3 = R_f/R_1$ the first coefficient becomes $R_f/R_1$ too, so $v_o = \frac{R_f}{R_1}(v_2-v_1)$ and a common voltage on both inputs cancels.

steps.prompt: Summing amplifier with an ideal op amp.

ask.prompt: Find the current through $R_2$ (from $V_2$ toward the op amp; negative if it flows the other way).
ask.explanation: The − input is a virtual ground, so $R_2$ has $V_2$ across it: $i = V_2/R_2$ = {{V2|V}} / {{R2|Ω}} = **{{I_R2|A}}**. The other input does not affect it.

ask.prompt: Which value of $V_2$ would make $v_o$ = 0 (all else unchanged)?

steps.prompt: Inverting amplifier with a T-network in the feedback path.

ask.explanation: $i = v_{in}/R_1$ flows through $R_2$, so the T node is at $v_t = -iR_2$. KCL there: $R_4$ carries $i + |v_t|/R_3$. Result: $\frac{v_o}{v_{in}} = -\frac{R_2 + R_4 + R_2R_4/R_3}{R_1}$ = **{{V_U1/Vin||3}}**.
Gain $-\frac{R_2+R_4+R_2R_4/R_3}{R_1}$ = {{(-(R2+R4+R2*R4/R3)/R1)||3}}, so $v_o$ = **{{V_U1|V}}**. A small $R_3$ gives a large gain without huge resistors.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current through $R_3$.
ask.explanation: The T node is at $v_t = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}v_{in}$ = {{-R2/R1*Vin|V}}, so $|i_3| = |v_t|/R_3$ = **{{abs(I_R3)|A}}**.
Overall gain $\frac{R_{f1}}{R_1}\cdot\frac{R_{f2}}{R_2}$ = {{V_U2/Vin||3}}, so $v_{in} = v_o/\text{gain}$ = {{Vt|V}} / {{V_U2/Vin||3}} = **{{Vt*Vin/V_U2|V}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the magnitude of the current through $R_2$.
ask.explanation: $v_{o1} = -\frac{R_{f1}}{R_1}v_{in}$ = {{V_U1|V}}, and the second stage's − input is a virtual ground, so $|i_2| = |v_{o1}|/R_2$ = **{{abs(I_R2)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: An ideal-op-amp calculation gives $v_o$ = −18 V for a circuit powered from ±12 V. The real circuit will output −18 V.
steps.explanation: The output cannot go beyond the supply rails; it **saturates** near −12 V (often a volt or two less). The ideal model is only valid while the output stays inside the supply range.

steps.prompt: Balanced difference amplifier: $R_3 = R_1$ and $R_4 = R_f$.

ask.explanation: The + input draws nothing, so $V_2$ drives $R_3 + R_4 = R_1 + R_f$: $i = \frac{V_2}{R_1+R_f}$ = **{{I_V2|A}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the current drawn from $V_1$ (out of its + terminal; negative if current flows into it).
ask.explanation: $v_- = v_+ = V_2\frac{R_f}{R_1+R_f}$ = {{V_R4|V}}, so $i_1 = \frac{V_1 - v_-}{R_1}$ = **{{I_V1|A}}**. The two inputs load their sources differently.

steps.prompt: Order the steps for analysing an ideal op-amp circuit.
items: Check that there is negative feedback
Write KCL at the inverting input with zero input current
Solve for $v_o$ and check that it lies within the supply limits
steps.explanation: The virtual-short rule only holds with negative feedback. The last check catches saturation: if the ideal answer exceeds the supplies, the output clips.

steps.prompt: Non-inverting amplifier with an ideal op amp.

ask.explanation: $R_f$ carries $v_{in}/R_1$ = {{Vin/R1|A}} (same current as $R_1$), so $P = i^2R_f$ = **{{P_Rf|W}}**. That power is supplied by the op-amp output, not by $v_{in}$.
$v_o - v_- = \left(1+\frac{R_f}{R_1}\right)v_{in} - v_{in} = \frac{R_f}{R_1}v_{in}$ = **{{abs(V_Rf)|V}}**.
